item.title: DR Congo: Ebola response cannot succeed without broader humanitarian effort | NRC
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

A more comprehensive and inclusive approach is essential if the spread of Ebola is to be halted, warns the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)

Press release

DR Congo Published 19. Nov 2026

Six months after Ebola was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), the outbreak remains out of control and continues to devastate communities.

Insecurity remains a major concern in affected areas, where regular violent attacks continue to cause displacement, hindering access to healthcare and disrupting contact tracing and the monitoring of Ebola patients. Violent conflict allows the virus to spread unchecked, with devastating implications for the population. Experience on the ground demonstrates that containing the virus requires more than just a health response. It also requires a broader humanitarian approach that puts community protection and recovery at the heart of its priorities.

Against this backdrop, maintaining access to essential services and strengthening infection prevention and control (IPC) are critical. In more than 100 schools, 25 health centres, and 10 communities, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) supports the installation of triage systems and handwashing facilities, the provision of hygiene supplies, and the adoption of good IPC practices. These interventions help create safer environments for children, teachers, patients and health workers, while strengthening institutional capacities to prevent and mitigate the risk of Ebola transmission.

At the community level, risk awareness and communication activities bring key messages closer to the population. Working directly with local communities is central to addressing concerns and misconceptions, encouraging protective behaviours, strengthening trust and allowing for the rapid uptake of recommended prevention measures.

“I am living proof that early action saves lives,” explained one Ebola survivor in Ituri during an interview with NRC staff.

“As soon as I recognised the symptoms, I sought medical assistance. This decision saved my life and helped protect my family, my colleagues and the wider community. We really need to make sure people understand how important it is to act early. Without community awareness, we cannot fight this virus effectively,” he added.

The impact of the outbreak also extends beyond the immediate risk of infection. The high levels of disruption and fear triggered by the outbreak can affect children's emotional well-being and ability to learn. Through its Better Learning Programme (BLP), NRC works with schools to help children manage stress and anxiety, maintain their concentration and continue engaging in learning despite the challenges they face.

“Responding effectively to Ebola goes beyond preventing the transmission of the virus. It is also about protecting children, safeguarding the future of entire populations, and supporting those who survive Ebola to safely reintegrate into their communities,” said Silvia Beccacece, NRC emergency response team leader in Ituri.

“Every day, our teams work alongside communities, engaging with people, listening to their concerns and mobilising them to play an active role in the response. Six months into this outbreak, sustaining these efforts is a shared responsibility, and our commitment must remain strong for as long as people need support,” she added.

As the outbreak evolves, it is essential that the response becomes more effective and more embedded in communities. Authorities, humanitarian organisations and donors all have a role to play in ensuring that community-based prevention and protection activities can continue. This requires sustained political attention, meaningful support for local engagement, and predictable funding. Maintaining these efforts is essential not only to contain the outbreak, but also to protect the lives, rights and dignity of the people and communities affected.

Notes to Editors:

  • The latest figures on confirmed cases and deaths are available here: DRC Ebola Bundibugyo - Epidemic Intelligence Dashboard
  • Among the 68 health zones affected by the outbreak, NRC operates in 19, contributing to infection prevention and control and protection efforts. NRC's interventions combine support to health facilities, schools, and communities, to strengthen hygiene, reduce exposure to the virus and promote safer practices.
  • The Africa CDC has repeated its view that the current outbreak remains out of control (Reuters)
  • The World Health Organisation has warned that insecurity remains one of the greatest obstacles to the current response (WHO)

For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:

NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329.

item.title: Gender Dimensions Of Ebola Preparedness And Response In Uganda
item.description:
Country: Uganda
Source: UN Women

Please refer to the attached file.

Uganda remains at heightened risk of Ebola virus disease (EVD) due to the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, escalating transmission in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and extensive cross-border movement and refugee flows. While the Government of Uganda has strengthened national preparedness through surveillance, risk communication, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination, the roles and capacities of local women’s rights organizations (WROs) and women-led organizations (WLOs) remain insufficiently recognized and supported.

Recognizing that Ebola outbreaks disproportionately affect women and girls due to existing gender inequalities, caregiving responsibilities and unequal access to resources, services and decision-making, UN Women conducted a survey to assess the preparedness, participation, capacities, challenges and priority support needs of WROs and WLOs. The findings aim to inform more inclusive, locally led and gender-responsive Ebola preparedness and response efforts in Uganda, while strengthening the contribution of women-led organizations to community engagement, protection, psychosocial support and

item.title: Uganda: National Gender Rapid Analysis for Ebola Bundibugyo Disease (EVD) Response
item.description:
Country: Uganda
Source: UN Women

Please refer to the attached file.

The Government of Uganda, through the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development (MoGLSD), conducted a Rapid Gender Analysis (RGA) to strengthen gender-responsive, inclusive and protection-sensitive Ebola preparedness and response efforts. The assessment examined how Ebola outbreaks and related interventions affect women, men, girls, boys, persons with disabilities, older persons, refugees and other at-risk groups differently, identifying barriers, vulnerabilities, capacities and priority needs.

The assessment covered nine districts and Kampala, including refugee settlements, and examined key areas such as coordination and participation, disease surveillance and referral, risk communication and community engagement, case management, psychosocial wellbeing, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), infection prevention and control, continuity of essential health services, protection, accountability and livelihoods.

The assessment was led by MoGLSD, with technical, coordination and operational support from UNFPA, UNHCR, UN Women, War Child and Oxfam, and collaboration with the Ministry of Health, district authorities, refugee leadership, health workers, community leaders and community members.

The findings and recommendations provide evidence to guide government institutions and humanitarian and development partners in strengthening Ebola preparedness and response planning, informing resource allocation, addressing gender and inclusion gaps, and promoting meaningful community participation, protection and accountability.

item.title: Amid pain caused by the floods, a Red Cross emergency clinic helps bring new life in Nepal | IFRC
item.description:
Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

By Fleur Verwer, IFRC Communications Coordinator for the Nepal Floods Emergency

---

The Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) emergency clinic had only just opened for the day when a pregnant young woman and her partner walked in. Her clothes were soaked, she was in severe pain, and she did not know what to do.

Reaching the hospital was not an option: floodwaters had swept away the bridge leading to it, and she could not cross the river.

Having heard about the Red Cross emergency clinic, she decided to go there in search of help.

Dr. Gyanendra Jora was on duty when the woman arrived.

“She was only 18 years old and clearly did not know what to do. She told us that her water had suddenly broken the day before,” he recalled.

For Dr. Jora, it was immediately clear that there was no time to lose. After a quick examination of the mother and baby, he arranged her urgent referral to a birthing centre, where she could be monitored and deliver safely.

Dr. Gyanendra Jora outside the Nepal Red Cross Society emergency field clinic in Bidur, where he worked for weeks after the floods.

Photo: IFRC

Less than half an hour after she arrived, she was on her way. Dr. Jora, together with a nurse from NRCS and a volunteer, accompanied her in a NRCS ambulance on the journey to an urban health centre approximately 25 kilometres away. She was already far along in her labor, so the timing mattered. Around 30 minutes later, the team handed her over to the birthing centre staff, made sure she was in safe hands, and only then returned to the clinic.

Three and a half hours later, a healthy baby girl was born.

When news of the birth reached the clinic, a wave of relief swept through the team that had made the first, decisive call.

Later, a team from the IFRC and NRCS, including IFRC Health Delegate Sachiko Kawase, visited the mother and her newborn daughter to see how they were doing. They found the baby healthy and thriving. To support the family in the days ahead, the team gave the mother a dignity kit, including a scarf for the baby, and a hygiene kit. It was the latest step in a chain of care: from the first examination and the ambulance ride to this follow-up visit, the Red Cross had accompanied the family at every stage.

Amid the grief, pain, and loss caused by the floods, a new life brought a spark of hope.

A member of the Nepal Red Cross Society examines a woman at the clinic, which treated more than 1,500 people in 24 days.

Photo: IFRC

A vital lifeline after the floods

The young mother’s story was just one of many that unfolded at the Red Cross emergency clinic in Bidur.

After the devastating floods on 26 August, the town was largely cut off from healthcare services. The bridge that connected the public hospital to the other side of town was washed away by the sheer force of the water. People who relied on the hospital for medication, free healthcare, or urgent medical assistance suddenly had nowhere to turn.

To keep essential healthcare within reach, the NRCS set up the desperately needed emergency clinic.

The clinic itself was not new, but it was just as vital as ever. It had first been deployed after the 2015 earthquake in Nepal. Once again, it provided a critical lifeline, making the difference between having access to basic healthcare and having none at all.

In the 24 days the clinic was open, doctors treated more than 1,500 people with a wide range of conditions, from minor health problems and chronic illnesses such as high blood pressure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to conditions requiring urgent referral to a hospital.

No two days were the same.

Yet every day, doctors, nurses, a pharmacist, and psychosocial support volunteers were ready to serve their community. For twenty-four consecutive days without a break, they served with a friendly smile and a dedication to helping others.

Nepal Red Cross Society members help two people affected by the floods at the clinic’s pharmacy.

Photo: IFRC

Supporting the community

Seventeen-year-old volunteer Isha was there from the day the clinic first opened after the floods.

“I live just behind the clinic. Luckily, my home was not affected by the flood, and my family is safe. When I heard the emergency clinic was being set up, I wanted to help immediately. I assisted the pharmacist and took some of the workload off his shoulders,” Ischa said.

Volunteers like Isha were not the only ones giving their all. Dr. Jora, who worked at the clinic for weeks, did more than treat patients: he also offered a listening ear, and he was deeply affected by the stories they shared.

“I knew I was there to provide medical care, but the stories people shared stayed with me. So many people were carrying so much pain. Not only physically, but emotionally as well,” Dr. Jora said.

He recalled one man who had suffered three seizures in quick succession, each lasting several minutes.

“He lived alone and was unconscious for hours. It was only days later that he came to the clinic. When I thought about the fact that he had to face that situation alone, without any help during such a frightening experience, it really affected me. And that was only one story. There were so many more.

“That is why I was grateful to be there for these people when they needed it most,” he added.

Isha, 17, who lives just behind the clinic, volunteered to help the pharmacist from the day the clinic opened.

Photo: IFRC

The path to recovery

The Red Cross emergency clinic was only one part of the Red Cross response. Working with national and local authorities and supported by the IFRC, the NRCS had used helicopters to deliver relief supplies to communities cut off by damaged infrastructure.

Where bridges had been washed away, NRCS volunteers helped people cross the river on a tuin, a simple trolley running along a rope line that carried people and everyday items to the other side, including on the way to the district hospital in Nuwakot. The NRCS had also restored access to safe water for more than 13,900 people and provided psychological first aid and psychosocial support to over 1,700 others. In Bidur, it was the first agency to begin providing cash assistance to families in need.

Behind this work was funding that was mobilized almost immediately: the IFRC released nearly CHF 1 million from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund the same day the floods struck, and a CHF 25 million Emergency Appeal, set to run for 24 months, followed the next day.

The long timeframe reflects how much remains to be done. Teams are still working to scale up shelter, clean water and sanitation, health services, psychosocial support, and cash assistance. Over time, the aim is to help families leave tents and evacuation camps for safer, lasting homes and to restore their livelihoods.

The story of one mother and her baby shows what timely help can do. To reach more families like hers, please consider supporting the IFRC Nepal Floods Emergency Appeal.

item.title: UNICEF Somalia Humanitarian Situation Report No.3, 1 July - 30 September 2026
item.description:
Country: Somalia
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

  • Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded.
  • UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

item.title: World: Resumen ejecutivo: Informe Alto a la guerra contra la niñez – Hacer posible un futuro mejor
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Please refer to the attached file.

INFORME ALTO A LA GUERRA CONTRA LA NIÑEZ - HACER POSIBLE UN FUTURO MEJOR

En la actualidad, uno de cada cuatro niños y niñas del mundo vive en zonas de conflicto, una cifra récord desde que se empezó a tener registro de esto en 1990. Una de las preocupaciones políticas y humanitarias más acuciantes de nuestros días es el sufrimiento de la infancia afectada por conflictos armados. Sin embargo, sigue siendo una de las cuestiones más desatendidas.

Los niños y las niñas sufren de manera desproporcionada durante los conflictos. Sus cuerpos pequeños, aún en crecimiento, son extremadamente vulnerables al impacto de los explosivos. Sus mentes, que aún están forjando su propia identidad, construyendo su sentido de seguridad y comprendiendo el mundo, viven el trauma de un modo diferente, que puede dejar huellas a largo plazo y afectar su desarrollo. Estos impactos pueden poner en riesgo toda su niñez y tener consecuencias que perduren más allá del fin de las hostilidades, atravesando, a veces, múltiples generaciones.

Durante los conflictos, aumenta el riesgo de vivir en la pobreza, las redes de apoyo se debilitan, y puede que los niños y las niñas sean separados de sus familias. Suelen interrumpirse los servicios básicos y cerrarse las escuelas, los niños y las niñas interrumpen su escolaridad y no logran las metas educativas, con el consiguiente impacto en su futuro. Alimentarse bien y acceder a servicios de salud esenciales puede convertirse en algo muy difícil, con un impacto devastador en la salud mental de la infancia y de quienes están a cargo de su cuidado.

El último informe de nuestra serie Alto a la guerra contra la niñez mide el nivel de exposición de los niños y las niñas a los conflictos y el daño que esto les genera. Se basa en el análisis de las violaciones graves contra la infancia documentadas por el mecanismo de vigilancia y presentación de informes de la ONU entre 2005 y 2025, que forma parte de los informes presentados anualmente por del Secretario General sobre los niños y los conflictos armados. Hemos complementado esta información con cifras actualizadas del Instituto de Investigación para la Paz de Oslo (PRIO, por sus siglas en inglés) sobre los niños y las niñas que viven en zonas de conflicto, entendidas como áreas situadas en un radio de 50 km de algún incidente relacionado con un conflicto en un año dado.

Veinte años después de establecido el mecanismo de la ONU, las cifras de violaciones graves contra niños y niñas en el contexto de conflictos armados siguen siendo extremadamente altas. Los sistemas de protección se encuentran al límite de su capacidad. El financiamiento humanitario está disminuyendo y algunos países están dejando atrás los compromisos asumidos en los tratados y los mecanismos de rendición de cuentas, en un momento en que son tan necesarios. No se presta la debida atención a las experiencias de los niños y las niñas, y las investigaciones que llegan a realizarse sobre las violaciones perpetradas suelen carecer de los recursos y el personal especializado necesarios.

El Derecho Internacional Humanitario confiere a los niños y las niñas un respeto y protección especiales. Sin embargo, la forma de hacer cumplir la ley y las herramientas utilizadas para proteger a la población civil están concebidas en torno a las personas adultas, y no tienen en cuenta las vulnerabilidades particulares de la infancia. Las nuevas formas de la guerra y las tecnologías emergentes generan mayores riesgos, que los sistemas de protección actuales aún no abordan de manera adecuada.

Para cerrar estas brechas, es preciso implementar sostenidamente medidas de prevención, respuesta y recuperación. Los ejemplos que se presentan en este informe, que surgen de las experiencias del personal de Save the Children en todo el mundo, muestran que es posible reforzar la protección cuando existen responsabilidades claras, se promueve la participación significativa de la infancia, y se dispone de personal capacitado, servicios que funcionan, un firme compromiso político, acceso a la ayuda humanitaria y financiamiento predecible.

item.title: World: Résumé du rapport : Stop à la guerre contre les enfants - Changer la donne
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Please refer to the attached file.

DU RAPPORT : STOP À LA GUERRE CONTRE LES ENFANTS – CHANGER LA DONNE

Près d’un quart des enfants à travers le monde vivent aujourd’hui dans des zones de conflit. Jamais encore un tel niveau n’avait été atteint depuis le début de cette comptabilisation en 1990. Les souffrances des enfants touchés par des conflits armés constituent actuellement l’une des préoccupations politiques et humanitaires les plus pressantes. C’est pourtant l’une des plus négligées.

Les enfants souffrent de manière disproportionnée durant les conflits. Leurs petits corps, en plein développement, sont particulièrement vulnérables aux conséquences des armes explosives. Leurs esprits, qui forgent encore leur image d’eux-mêmes, leur sentiment de sécurité et leur compréhension du monde, vivent différemment les traumatismes, avec des effets potentiellement durables sur leur développement. Ces conséquences peuvent mettre en péril toute leur enfance, avec des répercussions qui persistent bien après la fin des hostilités, parfois pendant plusieurs générations.

Le risque de pauvreté augmente, les réseaux de soutien sont affaiblis et les enfants peuvent être séparés de leurs familles. Les services vitaux sont souvent perturbés et les écoles fermées ; les enfants ratent ainsi des étapes clés de l’éducation, ce qui impacte leur avenir. Il peut aussi devenir incroyablement difficile de bien manger et d’accéder aux soins de santé vitaux. Tout cela peut avoir un impact dévastateur sur la santé mentale des enfants et celle des personnes qui s’en occupent.

Le tout dernier rapport de notre série Stop à la guerre contre les enfants montre à quel point les enfants sont exposés aux conflits et les préjudices qu’ils subissent. Il s’appuie sur l’analyse des violations graves commises contre des enfants documentées dans le cadre du Mécanisme de surveillance et de communication de l’information des Nations Unies entre 2005 et 2025, présentée dans les rapports annuels du Secrétaire général sur les enfants et les conflits armés. Nous avons rapproché celle-ci des estimations actualisées de l’Institut de recherche sur la paix d’Oslo (PRIO) portant sur le nombre d’enfants vivant dans des zones de conflit ; ce terme étant défini comme les zones situées dans un rayon de 50 kilomètres autour d’un conflit sur une année donnée.

Vingt ans après la création de ce mécanisme, le nombre de violations graves commises contre des enfants en situation de conflit reste exceptionnellement élevé. Les systèmes de protection sont sous tension. Les financements humanitaires sont en baisse et certains États se retirent des engagements pris dans le cadre de traités et des mécanismes de redevabilité, à l’heure où ils sont plus indispensables que jamais. Les expériences vécues par les enfants ne suscitent pas un grand intérêt et lorsque des enquêtes sont effectivement menées sur des violations, l’expertise spécialisée et les ressources requises font souvent défaut.

Le droit international humanitaire confère aux enfants un droit particulier au respect et à la protection. Or, les modalités d’application des lois et les outils utilisés pour protéger les civils restent largement conçus pour les adultes et ignorent souvent les vulnérabilités distinctes des enfants. L’évolution des guerres et les technologies émergentes créent des risques supplémentaires auxquels les mesures de protection existantes ne répondent pas correctement.

Des actions durables de prévention, de réponse et de rétablissement sont nécessaires pour combler ces lacunes. Les exemples présentés tout au long de ce rapport, qui s’appuient sur les constatations faites par le personnel de Save the Children à travers le monde, montrent que des responsabilités clairement définies, un personnel formé, des services qui fonctionnent, une participation significative des enfants, un engagement politique durable, un accès humanitaire et des financements prévisibles peuvent renforcer la protection.

item.title: World: Children affected by armed conflict, 1990–2025
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Peace Research Institute Oslo

Please refer to the attached file.

More children than ever live in conflict zones

Posted Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 by Gudrun Østby & Siri Aas Rustad

More children now live near armed conflict than the combined populations of the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Armed violence escalated sharply across the globe in 2025. Data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) shows that conflict-related fatalities rose to 244,600, up from approximately 187,000 in 2024. This made 2025 one of the deadliest years since the end of the Cold War. Much of the increase was driven by a dramatic rise in violence targeting civilians, particularly in Sudan.

While armed conflict affects entire populations, children are among those who suffer the most severe and lasting consequences.

Children face grave violations, including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. But the consequences of war extend far beyond direct violence. Children living in conflict-affected areas are more likely to drop out of school, lack access to clean water, and face heightened risks of death from illness, malnutrition, or lack of vaccines and medical care.

Today, Save the Children launches its new report, Stop the War on Children 2026. The report is based on PRIO’s tenth annual mapping of children in armed conflict covering the period 1990–2025.

Our latest estimates show that 589 million children, more than one in five of the world's children, were living in conflict zones in 2025. This represents a 7% increase from 2024, when an estimated 550 million children were affected. It marks a new all-time high both in absolute numbers and as a share of the global child population.

While the figures have fluctuated from year to year, the long-term trend is clear. The proportion of children living in conflict zones has more than doubled since the mid-1990s, rising from around 10% to 23.4% in 2025.

How we estimate the number of conflict-affected children

Most conflicts occur within limited, localized areas of countries. To estimate the number of children living in conflict zones, it is essential to isolate these areas. The UCDP Georeferenced Events Dataset (UCDP GED) provides precise data on the location of each separate conflict event or incidence of organized violence, including geographical coordinates. Using this data, we map circles with a 50 km radius around each conflict event and estimate the number of children residing within these areas based on population data from CIESIN and the United Nations. We define children affected by conflict as those living within 50 km of one or more conflict events. This 50 km radius is considered a reasonable distance within which conflict can significantly disrupt children's daily lives.

Key findings from the latest update

  • An estimated 1.5 billion children lived in a conflict-affected country in 2025. Of these, 589 million, more than one in five children worldwide, lived in a conflict zone.
  • 355 million children lived in high-intensity conflict zones (with 1,000 or more battle-related deaths) in 2025. This represents an increase of more than 11% from 319 million in 2024.
  • Africa had the largest number of children living in conflict zones, with 260 million. The Middle East had the highest share relative to its child population, at 40.2%.

What can be done to protect children in conflict zones?

Now, more than ever, the need to protect millions of children in conflict zones is urgent. While the devastating impacts of war in Ukraine and the Middle East continue to demand sustained international attention, the growing concentration of conflict-affected children in Africa underscores the need for greater focus on the continent. Africa is now home to 44% of the world's conflict-affected children, and humanitarian needs continue to rise rapidly.

Addressing the growing impact of armed conflict on children worldwide will require sustained commitment from governments, donors, humanitarian organizations, and local communities. Priorities include:

  • Invest in research and data collection to better understand how armed conflict affects children.
  • Ensure adequately resourced and high-quality peacekeeping operations in conflict-affected areas.
  • Partner with local peacebuilders and place children's needs at the centre of peace processes from the outset.
  • Establish and protect safe spaces where children can learn, play, and access essential services.
  • Strengthen accountability mechanisms, including credible sanctions against armed groups responsible for grave violations against children.
  • Increase support to conflict-affected countries to rebuild essential infrastructure, particularly education and health systems, at a time when aid budgets are under growing pressure.

For more information, read Save the Children’s full 2026 report, Stop the War on Children 2026. Available at: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/stop-the-war-on-children-changing-the-odds-2026

For a policy brief describing our update of the annual mapping of children affected by armed conflict, read our PRIO Conflict Trends Policy Brief 0X/2026: ‘Children Affected by Armed Conflict, 1990–2025’

item.title: World: Estado de la Población Mundial 2026: Generaciones venideras - Empoderar a la juventud para que trace su propio futuro
item.description:
Country: World
Source: United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

PRÓLOGO

Desde que se aprobó la Carta de las Naciones Unidas en 1945, el mundo se comprometió a "preservar a las generaciones venideras del flagelo de la guerra". Ha llegado el momento de que esta promesa vaya aún más lejos: las generaciones venideras también han de tener la oportunidad, la libertad y el poder de moldear el mundo que heredarán.

Este informe nos da motivos tanto para actuar con urgencia como para mantener la esperanza. Las personas jóvenes de hoy en día están mejor formadas y conectadas que cualquier otra generación anterior: innovan, emprenden, lideran movimientos comunitarios y actúan como agentes de cambio. Sin embargo, hay un porcentaje desproporcionado de jóvenes que, a pesar de su enorme potencial, se enfrenta a un horizonte de oportunidades cada vez más reducido.

El costo de la vida está aumentando; cada vez es más difícil encontrar un trabajo seguro y una vivienda asequible; los conflictos, el cambio climático y la desigualdad están transformando las vidas y las expectativas; los avances en materia de salud sexual y reproductiva no pueden darse por sentados; y son demasiadas las personas jóvenes que se ven excluidas de los espacios donde se toman las decisiones sobre su futuro.

Estas condiciones tienen repercusiones que van mucho más allá de las políticas de juventud, ya que influyen en algunas de las decisiones más trascendentales de la vida de las personas, por ejemplo, si pueden o no independizarse, encontrar un trabajo digno, formar una relación, tener hijos si lo desean y cuando lo deseen, y construir la vida que imaginan para sí mismas. El futuro demográfico dependerá, en última instancia, de millones de decisiones individuales de este tipo, así como de que las personas cuenten con los medios y las oportunidades necesarios para tomarlas libremente.

Apoyándose en las opiniones de más de 100.000 jóvenes, este informe pone de relieve que las generaciones actuales son perfectamente conscientes de las dificultades a las que se enfrentan, pero no tienen la menor intención de tirar la toalla. La juventud considera que los sistemas actuales pueden cambiar. Quiere sociedades más inclusivas y que rindan cuentas; economías que generen oportunidades reales; comunidades libres de violencia basada en género y discriminación; e instituciones en las que la participación permita influir realmente en las decisiones.
Lo más importante es que no están pidiendo a otras personas que construyan ese futuro por ellas; ya lo están construyendo por sí mismas.

He sido testigo de lo que personas jóvenes de todo el planeta son capaces de lograr cuando disponen del espacio, los recursos y el poder necesarios para llevar a la práctica sus ideas, y, a lo largo de estas páginas, podrán conocer la historia de algunas de ellas.

La juventud nos ha dejado claro, una y otra vez, qué es lo que le importa; la pregunta es cómo responderemos a lo que nos ha transmitido.

Nuestra responsabilidad es garantizar que sus aspiraciones se conviertan en opciones reales.
Esto implica invertir en salud, educación y oportunidades económicas para las personas jóvenes; implica proteger su capacidad de tomar decisiones sobre sus propios cuerpos y vidas; e implica hacer algo más que invitarlas a participar en el diálogo: debemos compartir con ellas la responsabilidad de la toma de decisiones.

El futuro no es algo dado, sino aquello que las generaciones construyen juntas.

Este informe lanza una invitación —y un desafío— para que empecemos a construirlo desde ya.

Diene Keita
Directora Ejecutiva
Fondo de Población de las Naciones Unidas

item.title: World: État de la population mondiale 2026 : Générations futures - Donner aux jeunes les moyens de façonner leur avenir
item.description:
Country: World
Source: United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

AVANT-PROPOS

Depuis l'adoption de la Charte des Nations Unies en 1945, le monde s'est engagé à « préserver les générations futures du fléau de la guerre ». Il est temps désormais d'étendre cette promesse : les générations futures doivent également avoir la possibilité, la liberté et le pouvoir de façonner le monde dont elles hériteront.

Le présent rapport nous donne à la fois des raisons d'agir de toute urgence et des raisons d'espérer. Les jeunes d'aujourd'hui sont mieux formés et mieux connectés que toutes les générations qui les ont précédés. Ce sont des innovateurs, des entrepreneurs, des leaders au sein de leur communauté et des agents du changement. Pourtant, malgré cet immense potentiel dont ils jouissent, ils sont encore trop nombreux à se retrouver confrontés à des perspectives toujours plus restreintes.

Le coût de la vie augmente. Il est de plus en plus difficile de trouver un emploi stable et un logement abordable. Les conflits, les changements climatiques et les inégalités transforment les vies et les attentes. Les progrès en matière de santé sexuelle et procréative ne peuvent être considérés comme acquis. Et trop de jeunes sont exclus des espaces où se prennent les décisions concernant leur avenir.

Ces conditions ont des répercussions qui dépassent les politiques relatives à la jeunesse. Elles influent sur certaines des décisions les plus importantes que les personnes auront à prendre au cours de leur vie : quitter le foyer familial, trouver un travail enrichissant, nouer des relations, avoir des enfants, si elles le souhaitent et au moment où elles le souhaitent, et bâtir la vie dont elles rêvent. Notre avenir démographique dépendra, en fin de compte, de millions de choix individuels de ce type, ainsi que de la mesure dans laquelle les personnes disposeront des moyens et des occasions nécessaires pour prendre ces décisions en toute liberté.

S'appuyant sur les points de vue de plus de 100 000 jeunes, le présent rapport dresse le portrait d'une génération lucide face aux défis qu'elle rencontre, mais loin de s'y résigner.
Les jeunes sont convaincus que les systèmes actuels peuvent changer. Ils veulent des sociétés plus inclusives et plus responsables ; des économies qui offrent de réelles perspectives ; des communautés exemptes de violence et de discrimination fondées sur le genre ; et des institutions au sein desquelles la participation permet d'avoir une véritable influence sur la prise de décisions. Surtout, ils ne demandent pas à d'autres de construire cet avenir à leur place.
Ils le construisent déjà eux-mêmes.

Partout dans le monde, j'ai pu constater ce qu'il est possible d'accomplir lorsque les jeunes disposent de l'espace, des ressources et du pouvoir nécessaires pour concrétiser leurs idées.

Tout au long de ce rapport, vous pourrez faire la connaissance de certains d'entre eux.
Les jeunes nous ont fait comprendre, à maintes reprises et sans ambiguïté, ce qui comptait pour eux. La question est maintenant de savoir ce que nous allons faire de ce qu'ils nous ont dit.

Notre responsabilité est de nous assurer que leurs aspirations deviennent de véritables choix.
Cela suppose d'investir dans leur santé, leur éducation et leurs perspectives économiques ; de protéger leur capacité à prendre des décisions concernant leur corps et leur vie ; et de ne pas seulement les inviter à participer aux discussions, mais de partager avec eux la responsabilité de la prise de décisions.

L'avenir ne se réalise pas tout seul, ce sont les générations qui, en agissant ensemble, le façonnent.

Le présent rapport constitue à la fois une invitation et un défi, qui nous incitent à commencer à le bâtir dès maintenant.

Mme Diene Keita

Directrice exécutive

Fonds des Nations Unies pour la population

item.title: State of World Population 2026: Succeeding Generations - Empowering young people to chart the future [EN/AR]
item.description:
Country: World
Source: United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached files.

UNFPA warns: the world risks letting the next generation down

A mix of economic instability, inequality, exclusion and other destabilizing factors are holding young people back from fulfilling their ambitions.

New York, 19 November 2026 — Young people have never been more educated, connected to information or aware of their rights. Yet for millions, the building blocks of adult life — a decent job, financial independence, a home, relationships, family and a say in their future — are becoming harder to secure.

The 2026 State of World Population report, Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future, published today by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), reveals a growing disconnect between the opportunities young people have gained on paper and the realities they face as they enter adulthood.

Many young people are coming of age amid economic insecurity, conflict, climate change, rapidly changing technologies and widening inequality. For some, independence, partnership and parenthood are being pushed later and later. For others, poverty and crisis force adult responsibilities far too soon. In both cases it is a generation trying to build its future in conditions that too often constrain the choices available to them.

“Young people want independence, stable relationships, and many want children. But too often, economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, conflict and exclusion are putting those aspirations out of reach,” said Diene Keita, Executive Director of UNFPA. “Our responsibility is to make sure their aspirations become real choices. That means investing in their health, education and economic opportunities. It means protecting their ability to make decisions about their own bodies and lives.”

The report demonstrates how historically high levels of education, unprecedented access to information, and major improvements in global health and human rights cannot guarantee a secure start in adult life, as economic insecurity, inequality and other destabilizing factors are stopping young people from shaping their own lives.

Climate change, conflict, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, and massive funding cuts to global health and development are all adding to the challenges.

These converging pressures are already shaping some of young people’s most personal decisions. UNFPA’s survey of more than 100,000 young adults across 73 countries and territories recently found that while they still want to find partners and have children, financial insecurity is making these milestones harder to realize: young adults are achieving independence from their parents in their late 20s, settling down in their 30s, and becoming parents as they near their 40.

When confronted by these challenges, young people are taking action: they are organizing in their communities, mobilizing online, taking legal action and joining public campaigns and protests. Young people consulted for the report were clear about what needs to change: they need better preparation for the future of work; decent opportunities to earn and become independent; protection of their bodily autonomy and reproductive choice; stronger health and social support; and a meaningful role in the decisions that will shape their lives.

The central message of Succeeding Generations is that global partners must do more to create the conditions that make life’s milestones possible. Giving young people the health, security, opportunities and influence to shape their own lives is not only an investment in one generation — it will help determine the societies, economies and families that succeeding generations inherit.

You can access the UNFPA report Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future here: www.unfpa.org/swp2026

Key facts and figures from the 2026 State of World Population report:

  1. 1 in 5 young people globally are not in employment, education or training.
  2. In low-income countries, 4 in 5 young adults do not have a secure paid job.
  3. Young women aged 15–24 are more than twice as likely as young men to be out of employment, education or training, while 49 per cent of young persons with disabilities are neither in school nor employed.
  4. Some 76 per cent of people younger than 30 surveyed by the UN Youth Envoy's Office said politicians do not listen to young people.
  5. The number of people aged 10–24 living within 50 kilometres of active conflict more than doubled from 164 million in 1990 to 340 million in 2022.
  6. Young people’s aspirations include partnership and family formation (from UNFPA’s survey of more than 100,000 internet-connected young people in 73 countries):
    1. 70 per cent said marriage was their ideal relationship arrangement.
    2. 91 per cent wanted at least one child.
    3. 73 per cent considered having a partner and children important life milestones.
  7. More than 40 per cent of survey respondents aged 35–39 who said marriage is ideal are unmarried.
  8. One quarter of 35–39-year-old respondents said they had fewer children than they would like for their age.
  9. Financial insecurity was the most commonly reported barrier to partnering (57 per cent of survey respondents) or having children (72 per cent of survey respondents).
  10. Survey respondents with the most optimistic outlook on the future intended to have 0.4 more children than the least optimistic respondents.
  11. Among 15–19-year-old girls who have had an intimate partner, nearly a quarter report ever having experienced physical or sexual violence from a partner.
  12. Mental health conditions now account for 19 per cent of the total disease burden among adolescents.
  13. Adults aged 30 and younger make up 19 per cent of the global population but hold just 2.8 per cent of parliamentary seats – and fewer than half of these seats are held by women.
  14. Official development assistance from OECD countries fell by 23 per cent in 2025 – the largest annual contraction on record.
  15. As international health and development financing contracts, as many as 22 million additional preventable deaths could occur, among people of all ages, by 2030.

Media contacts:

About UNFPA and the State of World Population Report:

UNFPA, the United Nations Population Fund, is the United Nations sexual and reproductive health agency, working to uphold the rights and choices of women, girls and young people across more than 150 countries and territories. It reaches millions of women, girls and young people with essential health services, protection from violence, and vital information about their bodies and rights. It also helps governments plan for changing demographics, to build inclusive and resilient societies.

The State of World Population report is UNFPA’s annual flagship publication. Published yearly since 1978, it shines a light on emerging issues in the field of sexual and reproductive health and rights, bringing them into the mainstream and exploring the challenges and opportunities they present for international development.

item.title: oPt: Beyond Compliance: Strengthening Environmental, Social, Governance and Technical Assurance in Fragile Contexts for Accountable Delivery and Sustainable Impact (Project Insight Note #17)
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: International Water Management Institute

Please refer to the attached file.

Wasudha Abeyrathna, Umar Liaqat, Stephen Fragaszy, Vidhisha Samarasekara

Abstract/Description

This Project Insight Note (PIN) shares lessons from the Al Murunah project’s pilot in Palestine, led by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and implemented with the Palestinian Hydrology Group (PHG), on strengthening environmental, social and governance (ESG) and technical assurance for physical works in fragile and conflict-affected settings. It describes a layered assurance approach that includes early partner due diligence, a living ESG risk register, multidisciplinary technical and safeguards reviews, quantity and cost verification, virtual field trips, and an independent engineering review when site access was lost. The PIN shows that ESG oversight works best when it is built into project design and followed through with corrective action and sustainability planning, helping to build trust and support the scaling of climate resilience investment.

item.title: World: EU and UNDP Expand Partnership to Strengthen Local Conflict Prevention and Peacebuilding
item.description:
Countries: World, Gambia, Guatemala, Mali, Moldova, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Sri Lanka, Yemen
Source: UN Development Programme

New phase of Insider Mediation programme will help local peacebuilders respond more rapidly to emerging tensions and prevent conflict.

November 17, 2026

New York and Brussels – The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the European Union (EU) have launched a new phase of their partnership on Insider Mediation (2026-2029), expanding support for local peacebuilders working to prevent violence, resolve disputes and build lasting peace in conflict-affected communities.

Building on the achievements of the previous phase (2023-2026), the renewed partnership will strengthen the capacity of insider mediators to respond to emerging tensions and support locally-led peacebuilding. A key feature of the new phase is a rapid response mechanism that will provide flexible funding and technical assistance, enabling mediators to act quickly when tensions arise or opportunities for dialogue emerge.

Insider mediators are trusted individuals with strong ties to the communities in which they work. Their local knowledge, relationships and understanding of conflict dynamics enable them to bring opposing groups together, facilitate dialogue and help resolve disputes before they escalate into violence. The programme places particular emphasis on strengthening the participation of women and young people in these efforts.

"Local peacebuilders play a critical role in preventing violence, fostering dialogue and sustaining peace in contexts where trust, relationships and local knowledge matter most," said Shoko Noda, UN Assistant Secretary-General and Director, UNDP Crisis Bureau.

"By investing in insider mediators, we are strengthening the capacities of those who are often the first to identify tensions and the best positioned to facilitate solutions from within their own communities."

The previous phase of the programme supported insider mediators across eight countries: The Gambia, Guatemala, Mali, Moldova, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Sri Lanka and Yemen. It also established a global Community of Practice bringing together more than 90 insider mediators, developed practical knowledge products, and helped prevent and resolve conflicts affecting thousands of people.

"The EU is partnering with the UN in supporting the work of Insider Mediators, whose presence within affected communities make it easier to detect local tensions and react quickly on the ground, stated Peter M. Wagner, Director and Head of Service for the European Commission's Service for Foreign Policy Instruments (FPI).

"By leveraging deep-rooted local trust, insider mediators can defuse emerging conflicts and prevent escalations before formal national or international missions have time to mobilize.”

Insider mediators achieved tangible results across diverse conflict settings. In Mali, insider mediators helped resolve local disputes over land and natural resources. In Yemen, they facilitated dialogue to address community conflicts over water. In Guatemala, the programme strengthened indigenous participation in dialogue processes, while in Moldova, it supported efforts to build trust across divided communities.

These experiences demonstrate how locally led mediation can help address tensions before they escalate, while strengthening the relationships and capacities needed to sustain peace.

The new phase will build on these achievements, providing continued support to insider mediators in existing programme countries while expanding opportunities for skills development, mentoring and peer exchange. Alongside the new rapid response mechanism, the programme will strengthen the recognition, protection and inclusion of insider mediators in wider peacebuilding efforts.

The partnership also contributes to a growing body of practical knowledge on locally led peacebuilding, including The Insider Mediators' Playbook, the Guidance Note on Amplifying Inclusivity, and The Insider: Stories of Building Peace podcast, which shares first-hand experiences and lessons from mediators working within their own communities.

The renewed collaboration reflects the EU and UNDP's shared commitment to investing in local capacities to prevent conflict, strengthen social cohesion and create conditions for sustainable peace.

Learn more: Explore the Insider Mediation Programme and The Insider: Stories of Building Peace podcast.

item.title: Ethiopia: Helping those caught in the middle of the conflict in Oromia
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Communities in several parts of Ethiopia’s Oromia region have been heavily affected by recent conflict and violence. Every day, people fear the impact of armed violence on their safety and livelihoods. The ICRC is responding to many humanitarian needs in the region, mostly in cooperation with the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS).

"We work in some of the most affected areas of the region, in East and West Wollega, Horo Guduru Wollega, Guji and Borena zones,” says Igor Moroz, deputy head of the ICRC in Oromia, based in Nekemte. “Our teams do their utmost to help restore access to essential services and reach those caught in the middle of the conflict.”

In partnership with ERCS we have supported tens of thousands of families in Oromia in recent weeks:

  • We donated medical supplies to support health facilities, benefiting over 125,000 patients and often enabling staff to conduct significantly more consultations. We renovated two health centres, while similar projects are under way at two other health facilities.
  • To ensure access to safe water, we restored over 300 hand pumps and installed solar power to upgrade pumps, boreholes and water systems. These works have benefited 90,000 people so far, and many more will be reached upon completion of ongoing projects.
  • To strengthen the resilience of communities, we provided agricultural tools to 7,000 farming families in East and West Wollega, and cash to help almost 2,900 families replace lost assets in East Wollega, West Wollega and East Borena.
  • In our efforts to help separated families restore or maintain contact with their loved ones, we contacted over 70 families in the region over the past two months.

Earlier this year, over 2,300 displaced people received assistance to address urgent needs in Angar village, Sasiga district, in the East Wollega zone. “When we met them first, these people had no possessions,” says Igor Moroz. “Working with ERCS, we also improved their access to clean water and sanitation.”

Despite the difficult security environment, the ICRC met several times with arms carriers, authorities, religious and community leaders to strengthen respect for international humanitarian law and other relevant rules. It also facilitated workshops in East and West Wollega to train first responders on the proper management of the dead.

In Ethiopia, the ICRC is attentive to emerging humanitarian needs related to conflict and violence, both in the areas where it operates and beyond. This includes Moyale and its surroundings in the Oromia and Somali regions, on the border with Kenya, where continuous clashes have resulted in a wide range of humanitarian needs. While the assessments and response are being led by other humanitarian organizations, the ICRC stands ready to help through its main partner, ERCS, in coordination with all those concerned, to ensure the most acute needs are covered.

“In Oromia, we see humanitarian problems rising and we do our best to respond to the affected people’s needs, but we cannot be everywhere,” says Igor Moroz.

item.title: Ecuador ENSO Floods 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDREC032)
item.description:
Country: Ecuador
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

01-11-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 1 November 2026, heavy and persistent rainfall associated with the ongoing El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon triggered flooding, river overflows, landslides and mudslides across several areas of Ecuador, causing damage to housing, livelihoods, road infrastructure, water systems, health facilities, educational establishments and other essential services. The impacts were particularly severe in the provinces of Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Galápagos, Santa Elena, Los Ríos, Manabí, Bolívar and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. As of 3 November 2026, more than 55,000 people and over 12,000 homes had been affected, while damage to transportation networks, water systems and basic services further increased humanitarian needs and access constraints in affected communities.

The emergency occurred within the context of a strengthening ENSO event. Oceanic and atmospheric monitoring conducted by the National ERFEN Committee identified elevated ocean heat content extending toward the eastern Pacific, positive sea-level anomalies of up to 45 cm in the central-eastern Pacific, 40 cm around the Galápagos Islands and 35 cm along the Ecuadorian coast, the propagation of warm Kelvin waves and a deepened thermocline. Sea surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 1+2 region reached up to +5.2°C above average, creating favourable conditions for above-normal rainfall and increasing the likelihood of severe hydrometeorological impacts across the country.

Anticipating these conditions, the Government of Ecuador progressively strengthened preparedness measures and, on 29 August 2026, the National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR) declared a nationwide Red Alert through Resolution No. SNGR-238-2026 due to the risk of flooding, landslides and other hydrometeorological hazards. Based on the forecasts and available lead time, the Ecuadorian Red Cross activated its ENSO National Contingency Plan and launched an Imminent DREF operation focused on anticipatory actions in Esmeraldas, Guayas, Los Ríos and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, including community preparedness, strengthening of Early Warning Systems, temporary protection of homes, safeguarding of water systems, risk communication and institutional readiness measures.

During October and early November, forecasted impacts progressively materialized and expanded geographically, resulting in recurrent flooding, river overflows, landslides and disruptions to essential services across multiple provinces. Assessments and official reports indicate that the scale, severity and duration of impacts now exceed the scope originally envisaged under the 45-day Imminent DREF operation, requiring a transition to a Response DREF. The operation will support affected populations through emergency response activities while maintaining anticipatory actions in at-risk communities where forecast impacts have not yet materialized.

According to forecasts issued by INAMHI, the ERFEN Committee and NOAA, which estimates a probability of more than 90 per cent that the current ENSO event could reach a very strong intensity, above-average rainfall is expected to persist during the coming months and into the 2026-2027 rainy season. Additional flooding, river overflows, landslides and damage to critical infrastructure and essential services remain likely, particularly in coastal provinces, low-lying areas and communities exposed to recurrent flooding and territorial isolation.
